title: Questions Inside Sentences
goal: Use embedded questions with Norwegian subordinate-clause word order.

objectives.statement: Use embedded questions with Norwegian subordinate-clause word order.

spans.value: Mina is meeting her colleague Jonas at Oslo Central Station. They are travelling to Lillehammer for a work seminar, but the train information has changed.
Vet du hvilket spor toget går fra?

blocks.translation: Do you know which platform the train leaves from?

spans.value: Nei, men jeg kan sjekke hvor vi skal gå.

blocks.translation: No, but I can check where we need to go.

spans.value: Kan du også finne ut om toget er forsinket?

blocks.translation: Can you also find out whether the train is delayed?

spans.value: Ja. Det står ikke her hvorfor avgangen er endret.

blocks.translation: Yes. It doesn’t say here why the departure has been changed.

spans.value: Jeg lurer på om vi har tid til å kjøpe kaffe.

blocks.translation: I wonder whether we have time to buy coffee.

spans.value: Først må vi finne ut hvor spor 12 er.

blocks.translation: First we need to find out where platform 12 is.

spans.value: Vent, nå ser jeg det. Jeg vet hvor vi skal!

blocks.translation: Wait, now I see it. I know where we need to go!

spans.value: Mina and Jonas need information, but most of their sentences are not direct questions. Mina does not simply ask:

en.value: Which platform does the train leave from?

spans.value: Instead, she places that question inside a larger sentence:

no.value: Vet du hvilket spor toget går fra?

en.value: Do you know which platform the train leaves from?

spans.value: This kind of question inside another sentence is an
embedded question (indirekte spørresetning)
. Embedded questions use Norwegian subordinate-clause word order.
A direct question stands on its own and asks someone for an answer.

en.value: Where is platform 12?
When does the train arrive?
Why has the departure been changed?

spans.value: An embedded question forms part of a larger sentence. It can follow expressions such as:

en.value: Do you know …
Can you check …
I wonder …
We need to find out …
She explained …

spans.value: Compare the direct and embedded versions:
Direct question

en.value: Where is platform 12?

spans.value: Embedded question

en.value: Do you know where platform 12 is?

spans.value: Direct question

en.value: When does the train arrive?

spans.value: Embedded question

no.value: Kan du sjekke når toget kommer?

en.value: Can you check when the train arrives?

spans.value: Direct question

en.value: Why has the departure been changed?

spans.value: Embedded question

no.value: Jeg lurer på hvorfor avgangen er endret.

en.value: I wonder why the departure has been changed.

spans.value: Notice the change in word order. In a direct question, the finite verb often comes before the subject:

en.value: Where is platform 12?

spans.value: In the embedded question, the subject comes before the finite verb:

en.value: Do you know where platform 12 is?

spans.value: For the taught cases where the question phrase is not the subject, the compact rule is:

en.value: where + platform 12 + is
when + the train + arrives
why + the departure + is

spans.value: When the question phrase is itself the subject, use this branch:

statement.value: Subject question phrase + som + finite verb

en.value: which train + that + stops

spans.value: The larger sentence may itself be a question:

en.value: Do you know where platform 12 is?

spans.value: However, the question inside it still has subordinate-clause word order. The opening words Vet du make the whole sentence a question; they do not turn hvor spor 12 er into a direct question.
When a direct question begins with a question word, the embedded question normally keeps that same question word.

en.value: where
when
why
how
who
what
which platform

spans.value: When the question phrase is not the subject, the important change is the word order after the question word. When it is the subject, the separate som pattern applies.
Where

en.value: Where does Jonas live?
Mina knows where Jonas lives.

spans.value: When

en.value: When does the seminar begin?

no.value: De må sjekke når seminaret begynner.

en.value: They need to check when the seminar begins.

spans.value: Why

en.value: Why is the train delayed?

no.value: Ingen forklarer hvorfor toget er forsinket.

en.value: No one explains why the train is delayed.

spans.value: How

no.value: Hvordan kommer de seg til hotellet?

en.value: How do they get to the hotel?

no.value: Jonas undersøker hvordan de kommer seg til hotellet.

en.value: Jonas investigates how they can get to the hotel.

spans.value: Which

en.value: Which train stops at Hamar?

no.value: Kan du se hvilket tog som stopper på Hamar?

en.value: Can you see which train stops at Hamar?

spans.value: The final pair contains som because hvilket tog is itself the subject of the embedded question. No direct-question inversion is removed in this pair; the embedded form uses subject question phrase + som + finite verb. At this stage, the learner only needs to use natural complete forms, not classify different kinds of subjects.

sections.title: A common mistake: keeping direct-question inversion

spans.value: A frequent mistake is to put the verb before the subject inside the embedded question.
Incorrect:

en.value: 'Incorrect: Do you know where is platform 12?'

spans.value: Correct:

en.value: Do you know where platform 12 is?

spans.value: Incorrect:

no.value: Kan du sjekke når kommer toget?

en.value: 'Incorrect: Can you check when arrives the train?'

spans.value: Correct:

no.value: Kan du sjekke når toget kommer?

en.value: Can you check when the train arrives?

spans.value: The incorrect versions copy the order of the direct questions Hvor er spor 12? and Når kommer toget? Once those questions are placed after Vet du or Kan du sjekke, the subject must come before the finite verb.
English sometimes helps because standard English makes a similar contrast:

items.value: Do you know where the station is?

spans.value: Still, Norwegian word order must be learned from the Norwegian sentence itself. The reliable check is to locate the embedded question word and then look for the subject before the finite verb.

sections.title: Questions answered with yes or no: use om

spans.value: Some direct questions do not begin with a question word. They can normally be answered with yes or no.

en.value: Is the train delayed?
Do they have enough time?
Does the train stop at Hamar?

spans.value: To embed this kind of question, use
om
, meaning whether or if.

no.value: Kan du sjekke om toget er forsinket?

en.value: Can you check whether the train is delayed?

no.value: Mina lurer på om de har nok tid.

en.value: Mina wonders whether they have enough time.

no.value: Vet du om toget stopper på Hamar?

en.value: Do you know whether the train stops at Hamar?

spans.value: Again, the embedded question has subject before finite verb:

en.value: whether + the train + is
whether + they + have
whether + the train + stops

spans.value: Compare the two types:
Information sought: A specific place
Direct question

en.value: Where is the hotel?

spans.value: Embedded question

en.value: Do you know where the hotel is?

spans.value: Information sought: Whether something is true
Direct question

en.value: Is the hotel far away?

spans.value: Embedded question

no.value: Vet du om hotellet er langt unna?

en.value: Do you know whether the hotel is far away?

spans.value: Information sought: A specific time
Direct question

en.value: When does the meeting begin?

spans.value: Embedded question

no.value: Jeg lurer på når møtet begynner.

en.value: I wonder when the meeting begins.

spans.value: Information sought: Whether something will happen
Direct question

en.value: Does the meeting begin soon?

spans.value: Embedded question

no.value: Jeg lurer på om møtet begynner snart.

en.value: I wonder whether the meeting begins soon.

spans.value: Use a question word when the missing information is where, when, why, how, who, what, or which. Use om when the underlying question asks whether something is true.
Norwegian subordinate-clause word order also affects words such as ikke. In a main clause, ikke usually follows the finite verb.

en.value: The train does not stop at Hamar.

spans.value: Inside an embedded question, ikke comes before the finite verb.

no.value: Vet du hvorfor toget ikke stopper på Hamar?

en.value: Do you know why the train does not stop at Hamar?

spans.value: Compare:

no.value: Hvorfor stopper ikke toget på Hamar?

en.value: Why doesn’t the train stop at Hamar?

no.value: Vet du hvorfor toget ikke stopper på Hamar?

en.value: Do you know why the train doesn’t stop at Hamar?

spans.value: In the direct question Hvorfor stopper ikke toget på Hamar?, the sequence is:

statement.value: question word + finite verb + ikke + subject

en.value: why + stops + not + the train

spans.value: The embedded question has:

statement.value: question word + subject + ikke + finite verb

en.value: why + the train + not + stops

spans.value: The same pattern appears after om:

en.value: Isn’t Mina coming to the seminar?

no.value: Vet du om Mina ikke kommer på seminaret?

en.value: Do you know whether Mina isn’t coming to the seminar?

spans.value: In natural conversation, the exact meaning of a negative question depends on context. The grammatical point here is narrower: when ikke belongs inside an embedded question, it comes before the finite verb.
More examples:

no.value: Jeg forstår ikke hvorfor bussen ikke kommer.

en.value: I don’t understand why the bus isn’t coming.

no.value: Kan du sjekke om hotellet ikke serverer frokost på søndager?

en.value: Can you check whether the hotel doesn’t serve breakfast on Sundays?

no.value: Hun spurte hvorfor døren ikke åpnet seg.

en.value: She asked why the door didn’t open.

spans.value: Do not confuse an ikke in the larger sentence with an ikke inside the embedded question:

no.value: Jeg vet ikke hvor hotellet er.

en.value: I don’t know where the hotel is.

spans.value: Here, ikke belongs to Jeg vet ikke. The embedded question itself is hvor hotellet er.

no.value: Jeg vet hvor hotellet ikke ligger.

en.value: I know where the hotel is not located.

spans.value: Here, ikke belongs inside hvor hotellet ikke ligger. This sentence has a different meaning.
An embedded question does not have to appear after a direct request. It can be part of a statement.

en.value: I know where the hotel is.

no.value: Vi må finne ut når resepsjonen stenger.

en.value: We need to find out when reception closes.

no.value: Jonas husker ikke hvilket rom møtet er i.

en.value: Jonas does not remember which room the meeting is in.

no.value: Mina er usikker på om de har bestilt lunsj.

en.value: Mina is unsure whether they have ordered lunch.

no.value: Ingen forstår hvorfor programmet er endret.

en.value: No one understands why the schedule has been changed.

spans.value: The whole sentence is a statement, so it normally ends with a full stop. Its embedded part still represents information that could be requested with a direct question.
Direct question:

en.value: Where is the hotel?

spans.value: Statement containing an embedded question:

no.value: Jeg vet ikke hvor hotellet er.

en.value: I don’t know where the hotel is.

spans.value: Direct question:

en.value: Have they ordered lunch?

spans.value: Statement containing an embedded question:

no.value: Vi må finne ut om de har bestilt lunsj.

en.value: We need to find out whether they have ordered lunch.

spans.value: The punctuation belongs to the whole sentence. Compare:

en.value: Do you know where the hotel is?
I know where the hotel is.

spans.value: Both sentences contain hvor hotellet er. Only the first sentence is itself a direct question.
Mina and Jonas reach the correct platform. A little later, Jonas prepares a message for the seminar organizer.
Nå vet vi hvor toget går fra, men vet du når vi kommer fram?

blocks.translation: Now we know which platform the train leaves from, but do you know when we arrive?

spans.value: Appen sier at vi kommer fram klokka ti over elleve. Jeg lurer på om arrangøren vet at toget er forsinket.

blocks.translation: The app says that we arrive at ten past eleven. I wonder whether the organizer knows that the train is delayed.

spans.value: Jeg kan sende en melding og spørre hvor vi skal møte de andre.

blocks.translation: I can send a message and ask where we should meet the others.

spans.value: Spør også om vi må gå rett til hotellet.

blocks.translation: Also ask whether we have to go straight to the hotel.

spans.value: A moment later, the organizer replies.
Hun svarer nå. Hun forklarer hvor vi skal møte de andre og avklarer om vi må gå rett til hotellet. Hun forklarer også hvor bussen stopper, men hun sier ikke hvorfor den ikke går helt til hotellet.

blocks.translation: She is replying now. She explains where we should meet the others and clarifies whether we have to go straight to the hotel. She also explains where the bus stops, but she doesn’t say why it doesn’t go all the way to the hotel.

spans.value: The situation has moved forward, but the same structure continues to be useful. Mina and Jonas use embedded questions to organize information rather than asking a series of isolated direct questions.
Notice the target forms:

en.value: when we arrive
whether the organizer knows

no.value: hvor vi skal møte de andre

en.value: where we should meet the others

no.value: om vi må gå rett til hotellet

en.value: whether we have to go straight to the hotel

spans.value: These two forms first express the requested information and then reappear in Jonas’s report of the organizer’s answer.

en.value: where the bus stops

no.value: hvorfor den ikke går helt til hotellet

en.value: why it does not go all the way to the hotel

spans.value: In each case, the subject precedes the finite verb. When ikke occurs inside the final embedded question, it precedes the finite verb går.
When writing an embedded question, use this short procedure:

items.value: Decide whether it begins with a question word or is a yes-or-no question.
Keep the question word, or add om for a yes-or-no question.
If the question phrase is not the subject, put the subject before the finite verb. If the question phrase is the subject, use subject question phrase + som + finite verb.
If ikke belongs inside the embedded question, put it before the finite verb.
Give the whole sentence punctuation that matches the larger sentence.

spans.value: For example, begin with:

no.value: Hvorfor går ikke bussen til hotellet?

en.value: Why doesn’t the bus go to the hotel?

spans.value: Place it after Hun forklarer:

no.value: Hun forklarer hvorfor bussen ikke går til hotellet.

en.value: She explains why the bus does not go to the hotel.

spans.value: The embedded sequence is:

en.value: why + the bus + not + goes

spans.value: For a yes-or-no question:

en.value: Does the bus go to the hotel?

spans.value: Place it after Vet du:

no.value: Vet du om bussen går til hotellet?

en.value: Do you know whether the bus goes to the hotel?

spans.value: The embedded sequence is:

en.value: whether + the bus + goes

spans.value: The next day, Mina is preparing to leave the hotel. She needs to ask reception about breakfast, checkout, and transport to the station. The setting has changed, but the information problem is similar.
Possible direct questions include:

en.value: When does breakfast end?

no.value: Kan jeg la kofferten stå her?

en.value: Can I leave my suitcase here?
Where does the airport bus stop?
Why doesn’t the key card work?

spans.value: Mina can make these questions part of longer, more connected sentences:

no.value: Kan du fortelle meg når frokosten slutter?

en.value: Can you tell me when breakfast ends?

no.value: Jeg lurer på om jeg kan la kofferten stå her.

en.value: I wonder whether I can leave my suitcase here.
Do you know where the airport bus stops?

no.value: Kan du sjekke hvorfor nøkkelkortet ikke virker?

en.value: Can you check why the key card doesn’t work?

spans.value: The grammatical decision remains unchanged. A question word is retained when Mina seeks specific information. Om introduces an embedded yes-or-no question. The subject comes before the finite verb, and an internal ikke comes before that verb.

The finite verb comes before the subject, copying direct-question order.

prompt.value: Build one complete station-scene question from the supplied tokens. Preserve both meanings: when the train arrives and which train stops at Hamar.

explanation.value: An embedded question uses subordinate order: question word/om + subject + sentence adverb + finite verb. Subject questions add «som», as in «hva som skjedde».

prompt.value: Choose the pair in which the first sentence asks where the hotel is and the second asks whether it is far away.

options.text: Vet du hvor hotellet er? / Kan du sjekke om hotellet er langt unna?
options.why: Hvor introduces specific location information; om introduces a yes-or-no question.

options.text: Vet du om hotellet er langt unna? / Kan du sjekke hvor hotellet er?
options.why: The meanings appear in the opposite order: om asks whether, while hvor asks for a location.

prompt.value: Write four natural Norwegian sentences addressed to hotel reception, one for each need: ask when breakfast ends; ask whether you can leave your suitcase here; ask where the airport bus stops; and ask why the key card does not work. Use a question word for specific information and om for the yes-or-no question. Put the subject before the finite verb in every embedded question, and put internal ikke before its finite verb in at least one sentence. Use your own wording rather than copying a complete lesson example.

prompt.value: Write in Norwegian a plain-language explanation of the embedded-question pattern and exactly two original sentences set in a hotel, workplace, or travel situation. One sentence must be a larger question introduced by a question word. The other must be a statement introduced by om. In the explanation, include subject-before-finite-verb order, the placement of internal ikke, and the subject-question pattern with som.

criteria.instruction: States in plain Norwegian that embedded questions use a question word or om, place the subject before the finite verb, place internal ikke before that verb, and use subject question phrase + som + finite verb when appropriate.
Produces one new larger question introduced by a question word with subordinate-clause word order.
Produces one new statement introduced by om with subordinate-clause word order.
Uses a new everyday situation and wording instead of copying a complete lesson sentence.
